title: Health, homes and heirs in Portugal
teaches: What health care costs an American in Portugal and what happens to Medicare, the taxes on buying, owning and selling a home, and what heirs pay

parts.title: The costs that aren't income tax

blocks.text: The last two lessons were about income tax, where Portugal is dearer than the US for most retirees. Much of the case for moving rests on everything else: health care, housing and daily life cost far less. This lesson goes through the large items that come with the move: health cover, Medicare, the house, and what happens to the estate.

A legal resident can register with the national health service, the SNS, and receive a user number.[^utente] Care through a local health centre and the public hospitals is then free or nearly so: most of the small charges for visits were abolished in 2022, and prescriptions are subsidised.

The SNS is good at serious and urgent care and slow at everything else, so most foreign residents add private insurance for faster appointments and private hospitals. Policies cost a few hundred to a couple of thousand euros a year at 50, far less than a US plan, rise steeply with age, and many insurers won't take a new client past about 65 or 70, or cover conditions they had before joining. Buying a policy early and keeping it matters more than the price in any one year.

Before 65 this replaces the most expensive line in lesson 11. A couple of 60 who would pay $24,000 a year for a benchmark plan in Washington, or lose the credit by crossing the cliff, pays a small fraction of that in Portugal, even with private insurance on top of the free SNS.
Medicare almost never pays for care outside the US. An American in Portugal still becomes eligible at 65, and has to decide whether to sign up anyway.

Part A, hospital cover, costs nothing for anyone with ten years of US work, so there is no reason to refuse it. Part B costs $202.90 a month each in 2026, more with a high income, and does nothing in Lisbon. Its value is as a way back: someone who skips Part B and later returns to the US can only join in a fixed window each year, and pays a premium raised by 10 percent for every full year they went without it (or without cover from a current US employer's plan), for life.[^penalty]

For a couple who might return when they are frail, keeping Part B, about $4,900 a year between them, is an insurance premium against that penalty. For a couple sure they are staying, it is $4,900 a year for nothing. Part D, Medicare's drug cover, and Medicare Advantage, private plans that replace Parts A and B, both need a US address, and Part D has its own penalty for joining late.

**Buying in Portugal.** The buyer pays a transfer tax, IMT, at a rate that rises in steps with the price, up to 6 percent, and a flat 7.5 percent of the whole price above about €1.1 million. A home that will be the buyer's permanent residence pays lower rates, and none on the first slice of the price. On top comes a stamp duty of 0.8 percent of the price.

**Owning.** The yearly property tax, IMI, is 0.3 to 0.45 percent of the property's tax value, set by the town within that range. The tax value is usually well below the market price.[^vpt] Holdings above €600,000 of tax value per owner also pay an additional tax, AIMI, of 0.7 percent on the excess, rising to 1 percent above €1 million.

**Selling the US house.** A US citizen keeps the US exclusion of $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a couple, for a home they lived in for two of the last five years, so the US would still exempt a sale up to three years after moving out. Portugal is the problem. It has no such rule for a foreign home: a resident who sells adds half the gain to their income at the progressive rates (Portugal taxes only half of most property gains). Portugal would credit any US tax on the sale, but the exclusion leaves no US tax to credit, so Portugal's is the whole bill. Selling before residence in Portugal begins, or in the US part of the year of the move, keeps the gain under US rules only, where the exclusion may make it free.

Portugal has no inheritance tax as such. It charges stamp duty of 10 percent on assets in Portugal that pass by gift or on death, but a spouse, a partner of two years, children, grandchildren and parents are exempt.[^partner] A lifetime gift of property in Portugal pays a separate stamp duty of 0.8 percent of its tax value, even to close family; inheritance doesn't. Assets outside Portugal, such as US brokerage accounts and IRAs, aren't touched.

blocks.text: The US estate tax goes on applying to a citizen's whole estate wherever they live, but only above $15 million per person in 2026, so few households meet it. A Washington estate tax return depends on being **domiciled** in the state, having it as your permanent home, or on owning tangible property there; the Washington branch's lesson on the estate tax covers it.

The bigger change than any tax is who inherits. Portuguese law reserves part of an estate, up to two thirds, for a spouse and children, whatever a will says. By default the law of the country where someone lived applies, but an EU regulation lets a foreigner's will choose the law of their nationality instead, which for an American means the law of a US state.[^choice] A will made in Portugal that makes this choice explicitly avoids a fight over which law applies.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A legal resident can use the SNS; most foreign residents add private insurance, bought early because insurers turn away new clients in their late sixties.
Medicare doesn't pay in Portugal, but skipping Part B carries a lifelong 10 percent penalty for each year missed if you return.
Selling the US house before the move keeps the gain under the US exclusion; after it, Portugal taxes half the gain at its progressive rates.
Close family inherits Portuguese assets free of stamp duty, and pays only 0.8 percent on gifts of property; other heirs pay 10 percent.
Portugal reserves part of an estate for spouse and children, unless a will chooses the law of the owner's nationality.

blocks.caption: Five questions on health, homes and heirs
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why might a couple living in Portugal keep paying for Medicare Part B?
choices: To avoid a lifelong late penalty if they return to the US
Because Part B pays for care in Portugal
items.why: Part B doesn't pay abroad. Its value is as a way back without a premium raised by 10 percent for each year without it.

items.ask: When is the cheapest time to sell the US home for someone moving to Portugal?
items.why: The US exclusion can cover the gain; after the move Portugal taxes half of it at its progressive rates, with no US tax to credit.

items.ask: A widow living in Portugal gives her Lisbon flat to her son during her lifetime. What does he pay?
choices: 0.8 percent stamp duty on the property
items.why: Children are exempt from the 10 percent, but the 0.8 percent on lifetime gifts of property applies to everyone.

items.ask: Does Portugal's 10 percent stamp duty apply to a US brokerage account left to a friend?
choices: No, it reaches only assets in Portugal
Yes, on all worldwide assets of a resident
items.why: The stamp duty on gifts and inheritances is charged on assets located in Portugal.

items.ask: How can an American in Portugal keep Portugal's reserved shares for spouse and children from governing their estate?
choices: By choosing the law of their nationality in a will
They can't: Portuguese law always applies
items.why: The EU succession regulation lets a will choose the law of the testator's nationality instead of the law of residence.

summary: **The SNS is open to legal residents.** Care is nearly free, and private insurance, bought young, speeds it up.
**Medicare stays home.** It doesn't pay abroad, but dropping Part B costs 10 percent a year missed if you return.
**Buying costs a transfer tax and stamp duty.** IMT reaches 6 to 7.5 percent of the price, and yearly IMI is 0.3 to 0.45 percent of tax value.
**Sell the US house before moving.** If it qualifies, the US exclusion covers the gain; after the move, Portugal would tax half of it at its own rates.
**Close family inherits free of stamp duty.** Others pay 10 percent on assets in Portugal, and lifetime gifts of property carry 0.8 percent for everyone.
**A will can choose US law.** Otherwise Portugal reserves up to two thirds of an estate for spouse and children.

utente.title: The user number
utente.text: Registration happens at the local health centre with a residence permit and a tax number. Waiting lists for an assigned family doctor are long in Lisbon and the Algarve, and shorter in smaller towns.

penalty.title: The Part B penalty
penalty.text: The general enrolment period runs from January to March, with cover from the following month. The 10 percent is counted for each full twelve months without Part B or cover from current work, and it applies to every later premium. Ten years abroad without Part B or such cover means paying double for the rest of one's life.

vpt.title: Tax value
vpt.text: The valor patrimonial tributário is set by a formula from the building's area, age, location and type, and revised every few years. It often runs at half the market price or less in older towns, though the gap is narrower for new flats in Lisbon.

partner.title: Partners who aren't married
partner.text: Portugal recognises a união de facto, two people who have lived together for more than two years, for several purposes, including this exemption. The US estate tax gives an unmarried partner nothing like a spouse's unlimited deduction.

choice.title: Choosing the law
choice.text: Regulation 650/2012 applies the law of the country where the person last lived, unless their will chooses the law of a country of nationality. The US has no single law of succession, so the will should name a state, and it should be made with a lawyer who knows how Portuguese registries treat the choice.
